ONE text with six gaps and SEVEN sentences: the extra one is a distractor, and the fact that a sentence used at gap 3 is gone for gaps 4-6 is most of the difficulty. That is why this shape replaces the old one, which gave every gap its own private four options and made elimination impossible — the exercise looked right and trained the wrong strategy. Paragraphs in `text` carry NUMBERED {n} placeholders matched to `answers` by index, so a renderer never counts gaps and one cannot drift onto the wrong question. `sentences` is the bank in the order it is shown; `answers[i]` is the index into it for gap i+1.
title: Cooking for the Camera
subtitle: An article about a props chef preparing food for films and television
text: Colin Capon has spent twenty years making food look right on screen. {1} The work is nothing like cooking in a restaurant, he says, because nobody is going to eat it.

Some films require a great deal of research. 'It's important that the food is as authentic as possible,' Colin explains. 'A hundred years ago you would never get a bowl of perfect fruit.' {2} Supermarkets stock most things all year round, but not always in the correct form.

The hardest jobs are the ones that have to survive a whole day of filming. {3} A wedding cake is the classic example: if it is cut before the director is satisfied, Colin has to go and make it look untouched again.
Heat is the enemy. Studio lights will wilt a salad in minutes and melt anything with butter in it. {4} Ice cream, famously, is usually mashed potato.
Actors are the other complication. {5} Colin keeps a bin beside the camera for exactly this reason, and has learned to cook things that taste of very little.
After two decades he still finds it satisfying. {6} It is a strange kind of cooking, but it is cooking all the same.
sentences: Without the use of chemicals they probably looked a bit marked and oddly shaped.
Everything has to be replaceable at a moment's notice, and identical to what came before.
A single scene can mean thirty takes, and somebody has to swallow every one of them.
He had never really paid much attention to what was on the plate before he started.
So most of what appears on screen has been built rather than cooked.
Nobody watching ever notices the food, which he takes as the highest compliment.
The pay was better than he had expected for what sounded like a hobby.
